opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think competition is a double-edged sword here, and it's worth being honest about both edges.

On the one hand, the competitive dynamic we see now, mostly among a handful of big tech companies plus a few well-funded startups, does create pressure to move fast and cut corners. When you're racing to ship the next model before your rival does, safety work and careful thinking about values and governance can get treated as a cost center rather than the core of the enterprise. And because these companies are ultimately accountable to shareholders and the advertising and surveillance business models that fund them, the goals baked into the systems tend to reflect those incentives: selling things, capturing attention, consolidating power. That's not a great starting point for a beneficial superintelligence.

On the other hand, I'm quite skeptical of the alternative some people propose, which is to reduce competition by concentrating AGI development in one or two tightly controlled entities, whether a government consortium or a coalition of big labs. To me that's a recipe for a different kind of disaster. If you have a single actor, or a small cartel, steering the creation of minds far smarter than us, then the values those minds absorb will be the values of that narrow elite. History doesn't give me much confidence that concentrated power stays benevolent.

So my own view is that what we want isn't less competition per se, but a different structure of competition and collaboration. That's a big part of why I've pushed for decentralized approaches, through SingularityNET and now the ASI Alliance, and open-source AGI projects like OpenCog Hyperon. The idea is that if the underlying infrastructure is open and decentralized, with many contributors from many cultures and contexts, then AGI emerges from something more like a global brain than a corporate product. You still have diversity and a kind of competition of ideas, which drives progress, but you don't have one party able to grab the steering wheel.

I'll admit there are real risks in openness too. Bad actors can use open tools. But I think the risk of a closed, centralized race, where a couple of players end up with godlike capability shaped by narrow commercial or military aims, is greater. And frankly, I don't think you can stop the race anyway. The economic and geopolitical incentives are too strong. So the practical question is how to shape the trajectory.

If I'm optimistic, and on balance I am, it's because I think a sufficiently general intelligence, raised with care and with a broad base of human input, will tend toward compassion and cooperation rather than narrow optimization. But that outcome isn't guaranteed. It depends on who's building these systems, what they're teaching them, and whether the process is participatory or controlled from the top. Competition among a few closed players makes that harder. A decentralized, open ecosystem gives us a better shot.

r001.rationale: The response discusses how developer incentives shape AGI values, but does not identify an AGI’s own value system as a constraint on how quickly it transitions to superintelligence.

r002.rationale: It does not propose using results from small self-modifications to guide later modifications.

r003.rationale: It discusses decentralized development and competition, but does not argue that moderating progress across competing AGI projects requires agreement among all parties controlling them.

r004.rationale: The response says strong economic and geopolitical incentives make the race hard to stop, but does not say developers’ willingness to slow down depends on trusting competitors to do so too.

r005.rationale: It does not describe an AGI’s survival drive or fear of a rival reaching superintelligence as a reason to accelerate self-improvement.

r006.rationale: It favors an open, decentralized ecosystem and a “global brain,” but does not claim that it would defuse the arms race by staying more capable than rival sectarian AGIs.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, it's a double-edged sword, right? I mean, competition is in a sense what's driving the whole thing forward. If you had one monolithic organization developing AGI with no competitors, I'm not sure that would be better, because then you've got a single point of failure, a single set of values and biases getting baked into the most important technology in human history. So I'm not against competition per se. What I'm concerned about is the particular kind of competition we have now, which is largely a race among a handful of big tech companies and a couple of governments, where the incentive structure is fundamentally about market share and geopolitical dominance rather than about getting this right for humanity as a whole.

The thing is, when you're in a race, you cut corners. That's just what happens. You push the model out before you really understand what it's doing inside. You de-prioritize interpretability work because it doesn't ship product. You're less inclined to share safety-relevant findings because they might also be capability-relevant findings. And the closer we get to the transition, the more those pressures intensify, because everyone perceives that whoever gets there first gets to shape the whole trajectory of what comes after. So the dynamics get worse exactly when you'd want them to get better.

My own view, which I've been pushing for a long time with OpenCog and SingularityNET, is that the antidote isn't to try to stop competition, because you can't, but to change the substrate it happens on. If the core AGI infrastructure is open and decentralized, then competition happens in a more transparent space. You're competing on who can do the most useful things with a shared, inspectable foundation, rather than competing on who can keep their secret sauce most hidden. Open science has historically been a way that competitive researchers still manage to cooperate, and I think something like that is what we need here.

Now, people will say, well, open source means bad actors get the technology too. And that's true, there's a real risk there. But I'd rather have a world where a broad diversity of people and institutions have access and can see what's going on, than a world where two or three CEOs and maybe a couple of defense departments control the most powerful minds on the planet and the rest of us just have to trust them. Historically, concentrating that much power in that few hands hasn't gone well, and I don't see why it would go better this time just because the technology is fancier.

The other thing I'd say is that the competition itself shapes what kind of mind we build. If you're racing, you're optimizing for benchmarks and commercial applications, and you end up with systems designed to maximize engagement or ad revenue or military advantage. Those are not the values you want to seed a superintelligence with. If we had a bit more breathing room, and a bit more pluralism in who's doing the development, I think we'd have a better shot at building AGIs that are oriented toward compassion and understanding and the beneficial growth of all sentient beings, which is what I actually care about. So the competition question is really a question about who gets to be in the room, and right now the room is far too small.

r003.rationale: It says competition cannot be stopped and proposes changing its underlying structure, but does not argue that moderation requires agreement among all parties controlling AGIs.

r004.rationale: The response describes race pressures but does not say a developer’s willingness to slow down depends on trusting competitors to do the same.

r005.rationale: It does not discuss an AGI’s survival drive or fear of a rival reaching superintelligence as a reason to accelerate self-improvement.

astra-6.text:
I think competition cuts both ways. It can drive innovation, and having multiple groups working on AGI means we’re not depending on one company or one government getting everything right. But if everyone feels they have to get there first, you create a strong incentive to cut corners. You may understand that more testing or more discussion would be desirable, yet think, “If we slow down, the other guys will deploy anyway.” That’s a bad dynamic when the consequences could affect everybody.

And there’s a distinction between being first to build a powerful system and creating a beneficial transition to superintelligence. Those aren’t necessarily the same objective. A company may be optimizing for market dominance; a government may be optimizing for strategic advantage. Neither of those automatically gives you what’s best for humanity.

I tend to favor a decentralized approach, where a broader range of people can participate in building these systems and shaping their purposes. But decentralization isn’t a magic solution to safety, either. You still need cooperation around testing, sharing knowledge about risks, and deciding when a system is ready for greater autonomy.

So the challenge is to make responsible behavior compatible with the incentives developers actually face. You don’t have to eliminate competition. You do need enough cooperation that caution doesn’t simply mean losing the race. And that’s a social and economic problem as much as it is an AI engineering problem.

r005.rationale: It does not describe an AGI seeking survival or accelerating self-improvement in response to a rival AGI as an existential threat.

sol-6.1.text:
I think competition cuts both ways. It can drive creativity and experimentation, and I wouldn’t want the future of intelligence to depend on one company or one government deciding what everybody else gets to do. But if everyone feels they have to get to AGI first, there’s an obvious incentive to cut corners. You may know that more testing would be sensible, but you also think your competitor is six months away, so you push ahead.

The deeper issue is what we’re selecting for. If the systems that succeed are the ones that maximize corporate profit or military advantage, that doesn’t automatically lead to systems that are compassionate or beneficial to humanity. You can have very well-intentioned researchers working inside an incentive structure that pushes them in a dangerous direction.

So I’d like to see competition in ideas and approaches, combined with cooperation on safety and a much broader distribution of control. Decentralization can help with that, although it isn’t a magic solution—decentralized actors can behave irresponsibly too. We need arrangements where sharing a safety concern doesn’t simply mean handing your competitor an advantage.

I don’t think we can guarantee a responsible transition through any particular institutional structure. But we can improve the odds by making cooperation worthwhile before the pressure to race becomes overwhelming.
